title: The hand that points to the foot
hook: one arm swings across the body like an elephant's trunk and points at a lifted foot: why Hindus bow at the feet
carry: his lifted foot is grace; refuge is at his feet
tomorrow: who is the little figure under Shiva's foot?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: samhara, the ending is God's work too, the flame held level with the drum. Today, the lower hands, and where one of them points.
screen: `THE BEGINNING IN ONE HAND, THE ENDING IN THE OTHER.` · `TODAY: WHERE THE HAND POINTS.`

segments.voice: A guide at a busy train station doesn't take your suitcase or drag you to the platform. She lifts an arm and points: that way. Then she lets you walk. Nataraja has a hand like that. Of his two lower hands, one is raised palm out, the do-not-fear gesture from the mudras. The other is the one to watch today. It swings across his chest and hangs loose, and the fingers point down and across the body, at his raised foot.
screen: `A GUIDE WHO POINTS: THAT WAY.` → `ONE LOWER HAND: DO NOT FEAR.` → `THE OTHER POINTS AT THE FOOT.`

segments.voice: That arm has a name in the language of dance: gaja hasta, the elephant hand, because it hangs across the body the way an elephant's trunk swings. Notice what the hand doesn't do. It doesn't hold anything, or grab, or push. It points, at the lifted foot. One foot is planted, pressing down; what's under it comes tomorrow. The other foot is lifted clear of the ground. In the usual reading, the planted foot presses down and holds, and the lifted foot is grace: release, the way out. Here is grace, says the hand. Look there. And that's the teaching behind a gesture you'll see in any Hindu family. The feet of the divine are where grace is, so they're where you bow. In temples, flowers are laid at the god's feet. In devotional poetry, taking refuge at the Lord's feet means surrender, trust, coming home. And because parents, elders and teachers are honored as people that blessing flows through, children bend and touch their feet, and get a hand on the head in return. The Tamil poet-saint Appar sang of this foot. In paraphrase: if you could see the arched brow, the smile, the matted hair and the lifted golden foot of the dancer, being born a human would be worth it. So when a kid touches a grandmother's feet before an exam, that's the pointing hand, at home: grace is there; bow there. The hand doesn't drag you. It points, and leaves the walking to you.
screen: `GAJA HASTA, THE ELEPHANT HAND.` · `IT DOESN'T GRAB. IT POINTS.` · `THE LIFTED FOOT: GRACE, RELEASE.` · `WHY HINDUS BOW AT THE FEET.` · `APPAR: WORTH BEING BORN FOR.` · then, large: `GRACE IS THERE. BOW THERE.`

segments.voice: If an elder is near you today, a parent, a grandparent, a teacher, you might bend and touch their feet, or bow to them in your heart. Then rest your left arm loosely across your lap, fingers pointing down, and follow its line to your feet. Feel one foot planted, let the other feel light, and breathe there. If you pray, bring your thoughts to the feet of Shiva, or of God.
Nataraja, the king of dancers. Today, the gaja hasta, the elephant hand that swings across the body and points to the lifted foot: grace, and the place to bow.
Your line: his lifted foot is grace; refuge is at his feet. That's why Hindus bow there. Back tomorrow, same hill.
